lesson.title: Three States, One Tug of War
lesson.summary: The state of matter a substance adopts, solid, liquid, or gas, is decided by a competition between the kinetic energy of its particles and the intermolecular forces trying to hold those particles together.
lesson.body:
Matter typically exists in one of three familiar states: solid, liquid, or gas. Each state is defined by how its particles, whether atoms, molecules, or ions, are arranged and how freely they move relative to one another. In a solid, particles are packed closely together in fixed positions, able only to vibrate in place, which gives solids a definite shape and a definite volume. In a liquid, particles remain close together but can slide past one another, giving liquids a definite volume but a shape that conforms to their container. In a gas, particles are far apart and move independently at high speed, so gases have neither a definite shape nor a definite volume, expanding to fill whatever container holds them.

What decides which of these three arrangements a substance adopts at a given moment is a direct competition between two things you have already studied separately: the kinetic energy of the particles, which comes from thermal energy and drives particles to move and spread apart, and the intermolecular forces between particles, which pull particles together and resist that spreading. Temperature is essentially a measure of average kinetic energy, so raising temperature increases particle motion and pushes a substance toward a more disordered state, while intermolecular forces constantly pull in the opposite direction, trying to hold particles in an ordered, closely packed arrangement.

This tug of war explains why the same substance can occupy any of the three states depending on temperature. Water at minus 20 degrees Celsius is ice, a solid, because the particles' kinetic energy is too low to overcome the extensive hydrogen bonding network holding water molecules in a rigid lattice. Warm that same water to 25 degrees Celsius and it becomes liquid, because the added kinetic energy lets molecules slide past each other while the hydrogen bonds still hold them relatively close. Heat it further to 105 degrees Celsius and it becomes steam, a gas, because the kinetic energy of the molecules now overwhelms the hydrogen bonds almost entirely, and the molecules fly apart from one another.

The relative strength of a substance's intermolecular forces also predicts, at a given temperature, which state it is likely to be in compared to another substance. Substances with weak dispersion forces only, like methane, tend to be gases at room temperature because comparatively little kinetic energy is needed to separate their particles. Substances with hydrogen bonding, like water, or ionic bonding, like sodium chloride, need much more thermal energy before their particles can escape each other's attraction, so they remain liquid or solid at temperatures where a dispersion-only substance would already be a gas. Keeping both halves of this competition in view, kinetic energy pushing apart and intermolecular forces pulling together, is the foundation for understanding phase changes, and it sets up kinetic molecular theory, which describes the motion side of this picture in more quantitative detail.
